rv.q: Now it shifts, aptly, to London, where the boy’s father would forge his success, enforcing his absence from the family home — to critical effect when illness strikes down his children. On stage we get droll glimpses of the writer’s London life, as he struggles with deadlines, debts and distracted actors.
This is a solid, elegant piece of storytelling that challenges the idea that genius is ever the work of one person alone.

Cabey (who also plays Hamlet) and Jarrett convince as adult actors playing avid adolescents. Chakrabarti’s enjoyable theatre-set scenes flag Shakespeare’s use of doubling characters. Hearts should crack at the concluding scene, but while this staging loyally recreates O’Farrell’s characters, it lacks her novel’s emotional impact.
It's hard to warm to a production so lacking in verve and energy.
But this adaptation is a palpable miss...the character feels overexposed here, which really drains the book's brilliant final scene of power.
This stripping back leaves us with some half-formed characters.
Whyman’s tight direction keeps the story moving at the right pace and still manages to acknowledge the structure of the novel.
All this, inevitably, is lost. Which wouldn't matter if the production had found inventive alternatives.

cn.t: Critics find this RSC adaptation of Maggie O'Farrell's bestseller disappointing, lacking the verve and emotional power of the source material, with too much left unsaid despite the novel's literary success.
